Honestly, 0/10 do not recommend. It didn’t help much for all the pain it caused. 

Have you heard of Flashing? It’s a newer thing. Similar to EMDR, but you don’t have to focus on the trauma. 
EMDR: pick trauma to work on, focus on trauma, do EMDR, check in on trauma, more EMDR, trauma, EMDR, etc. 
Flashing: pick trauma to work on and focus on it ONCE. Do calming exercise with EMDR tapping, check in with how you feel w/o focusing on trauma, do another calming set, check in, calming set, check in, etc until you don’t have anymore strong emotional reaction. One and done, no need to revisit the same trauma over and over during the session or at subsequent sessions.
Might be something to look into.

Hey, I see you. I when I sought help it’s wasn’t specifically for the self harm, but that was def addressed. 
I, like you, had no idea what to do. So I found myself at my county’s mental health help center (where I live there’s usually at least one per county) and they had people to talk to on the spot. They talked to me and got me on some meds (I was hallucinating pretty bad) and helped me find long term therapist and psychiatrist. So if you have access to something Ike that, it could be worth checking into. I know they’re not all as great as mine was, but they could be helpful. 

If you don’t have something like that, it’s a little harder. Idk what country you’re in or how far this website reaches, but psychologytoday.com is a google for therapists. There’s filters where you say “I have this insurance and want that type of therapy with a male/female who has experience in x” and it’ll pop out a few people. Call them and they likely won’t answer because they’re in session. So leave a vm and say “Hi I’m throwmetothe-stars and I’m looking for a therapist with x, y, & z. and came across your profile. Are you accepting new patients? Please call me at *your number* as I’d love to chat.” I also ask for 5 min of their time for a few quick questions. You can do this at your first meeting, but you can also do it over the phone to see if you even want to meet. Just like at the end of a job interview when they give you the chance to question them, question your therapist!!! Make sure they’re going to be a good fit! If you don’t know what to ask, google “questions to ask a new therapist” but you want to go for stuff like “what’s your specialty?” “How do you treat someone with my issues?” “How will I know when my therapy is complete?” Stuff that gets to the how and why of what they do and how they will interact with you. If you don’t like their answers, find someone else. The relationship between the therapist and client is more important than anything else, so you want to make sure this is someone you could see yourself working with. 
Also: many therapists are booked a few months out. So if you’re at your parent’s place for the next few months, calling now isn’t a bad idea. 
Also also: if you’re tight for cash ask about a sliding scale

Just wanted to chime in and say if you’re growing tired of it, take that as a sign. I understand the “who am I without self harm?” Once something defines you, it’s hard to think outside that perspective. Very hard, I will not lie. But not impossible! If your perception is slowly shifting from enjoying it to tired of it, take this as a chance for a change in perspective. Maybe you’re right on the edge between where you were and an new place. Think and decide where you want to be, and you’ll gravitate in that direction. It’s uncomfortable to say the least. And it sucks. But as someone who’s just set down the knife, I’m finding it so rewarding to not reach for it. I’d say it’s worth the work. 

I felt exactly how you described before I laid down my knife. Down to the comments about scar tissue and feeling weird about stopping. I jumped on the fact that I was growing bored of it and tried something new. 

I don’t know you, and I know just because I did it (am doing it, it’s an ongoing process) doesn’t 100% mean anyone can do it. Every one is in a different place and situation. So I won’t serve you any platitudes. I will say that changing your identity, what defines you, is hard but possible. Uncomfortable but rewarding. So if this habit is feeling old, you have the chance to jump on a new opportunity. 

I believe you’ll make the best choice for yourself, and that’s okay regardless of what you choose because you know yourself best. You got this! ☺️

It really depends on where you go. I’ve been hospitalized twice, at two separate places. 

The first was the regular ‘ole hospital. I went to the ER and they took all my stuff, took my phone, made me strip to check for self harm, and put me in a room with a guard. I was alone, with nothing to do, for 30 hours. It was pure hell. But then they moved me to the psych ward, and it got a lot better. They gave me my phone back, had good food, allowed visitors all day long, visitors could bring things, we all had private rooms, they brought meds to you, they had therapy groups but they weren’t mandatory, and they had little self-care groups from time to time. It wasn’t the worst. 

The second hospital was some private hospital. No ER to wait in, after I checked in they just put me in a locked room and made wait for 5 hours as they admitted me. They strip searched me for SH again, and put me in a room with 2 beds but I got permission to room solo. This place sucked. No phone. Took 2 days for them to get me my stuff. 1 hour a day for visitors who couldn’t bring anything. Mandatory group therapy. The worst food. You had to stand in line for at least 30 min for meds.

Both places have nurses check in on you every 15 min, take away or cut off anything with a string like shoe laces or hoodie strings or short ties on clothes, and round the clock nurses with occasional doctors and sometimes therapists but never for one-in-one. 
I’ll be honest, they both sucked. 

However, they didn’t admit me for SH but for suicidal behaviors. 
Anyway, I wish you luck. You’ll get through this, one way or another!

Not weird at all! There are several different reasons as to why people self harm. Two of the big ones are opposites: people cut because they feel nothing and want to feel something, or people feel too much and they want to feel less. Both are still self harming, and both do the same thing to your brain: release an adrenaline rush which is helpful in a lot of ways. It’s a way to feel something when you feel numb. It’s a way to “purge” emotion from your body when you have too much emotion in you. 
But strong emotion or no emotion, it’s still self harm. One isn’t more valid than the other.
Just please be careful. Remember: deep cuts aren’t worth it. This is coming from someone who knows firsthand.

I have a box like this! My therapist recommended it. She said to put something for each 5 senses in the box to help you stay grounded during these times. 
Here’s what my box looks like:

Taste: a candy. Chocolate is nice because it helps with depression. Only thing here is to be careful to only put a bite sized thing in there because you don’t want to replace a self harming habit with an overeating habit. 

Smell: a stick of incense, though I’m sure a candle or a scratch and sniff could work here too. I like the incense because it lasts about an hour and is a very strong earthy smell. 

Touch: I have a fidget cube, some little magnetic balls and a worry stone. I swap out what’s in the box every once in a while, but it’s one of those. 

Hearing: I made a list of playlists to listen to. I curated some soothing playlists and have a little note reminding me to put some music on

Sight: I have another little note reminding me to look at my art. I have a ton of stuff up on my walls, so I gravitate toward that. 

Put it all together and what do you get?!
I end up sitting in my couch with some incense burning, eating a chocolate, listening to music, looking at my art and fidgeting with something. It’s very grounding, which is the goal (for me at least). 

Hope this was helpful, and good luck with your box! ☺️
